Important context: there is EXISTING precedent for this in commit 1be40b0 "Add generated editorial imagery: home hero, mission, flagship projects, volunteers (#21)" — it added `frontend/public/images/generated/*.jpg` (duotone night/gold-graded photographs, generated, deliberately anonymous — no named team/board member depicted), wired into optional CMS fields in `frontend/data/seed.json` (`home.heroImage`, `about.mission.image`, `projects.items[...].image` for third-eye-kit and third-eye-world, `volunteers.heroImage`), each guarded by a `isSafeImageUrl` cast so clearing the field reverts to the pre-imagery look with no code change. Read that commit (`git show 1be40b0`) and the current state of the files it touched, to understand the established wiring pattern (where `isSafeImageUrl` is defined, how each page/component conditionally renders the image, and the CSS classes involved).

Then find every OTHER place across the site that is missing equivalent imagery:
1. `frontend/data/seed.json` — grep every `"img"`, `"image"`, `"heroImage"`, `"photo"`-style field. List which ones are empty strings, missing entirely for an item that has siblings with images, or the two remaining "Five projects. One ecosystem." items (`items` array under whatever section that is) that DIDN'T get an image in PR #21 (only third-eye-kit and third-eye-world did, per the commit message — check which items exist and which of them still lack an `image` field).
3. The `documents.blogs` array (`eye-of-the-heart`, `third-eye-kit`, `third-eye-kit-v2`) — confirm none of these have an image field and that `DocCard.tsx` / `doc-hero` currently renders only a gradient + inline SVG icon for all of them (no photo).
4. Any other page (Media page, About page sections beyond mission, Volunteers sections beyond hero, Donate page) that has an obviously blank/generic visual slot — check page.tsx files under `frontend/app/*` for hero sections or card grids that render icon-only or no-image placeholders.
5. Confirm the exact target dimensions/aspect ratios used for existing generated images (check the CSS for `.doc-hero`, `.page-hero--photo`, project hero, mission image, home hero) so new images can be generated at matching aspect ratios.

Report back: a concrete list of "field path → what's missing → suggested subject matter for the image → target aspect ratio", plus the exact `isSafeImageUrl` function location and definition, and the exact JSX pattern used to wire an image into a component (quote a real example, e.g. the mission image or a project hero). Keep the report organized as a checklist. Under 600 words plus the isSafeImageUrl code snippet and one wiring example.

simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

Three integrated components — glasses, shoes, gloves — each handle a different layer of the navigation problem.

Glasses detect upper-body obstacles: tree branches, signs, doorframes, people walking toward you.
Shoes detect ground-level hazards: curbs, holes, steps, objects underfoot.
Gloves carry ultrasonic sensors for navigating stairs, sensing surfaces, and reading terrain by hand — the user climbs by feel, not faith.

All three components connect to GPS. Live location is transmitted to family or caregivers. The kit detects falls and physiological distress and sends emergency alerts when something goes wrong. The system is deliberately low-fidelity. There is no camera. There is no machine-learning model running in the cloud. The kit works offline, works on old hardware, and works in places where any of those dependencies would fail. A trusted contact (family member, caregiver) receives live location and an alert if the system detects a fall or physiological distress. The user controls who sees what.

Three integrated components — glasses, shoes, gloves — each handle a different layer of the navigation problem.

Glasses detect upper-body obstacles: tree branches, signs, doorframes, people walking toward you.
Shoes detect ground-level hazards: curbs, holes, steps, objects underfoot.
Gloves carry ultrasonic sensors for navigating stairs, sensing surfaces, and reading terrain by hand — the user climbs by feel, not faith.

All three components connect to GPS. Live location is transmitted to family or caregivers. The kit detects falls and physiological distress and sends emergency alerts when something goes wrong. It works on 2G networks, which means it works in rural villages, dense urban environments, and anywhere in between. Distance readings translate into vibration patterns the user learns over a short training period — closer obstacles produce stronger, faster pulses; clear paths produce nothing. The components communicate over Bluetooth and connect through a paired phone for GPS, alerts, and remote monitoring.

The system is deliberately low-fidelity. There is no camera. There is no machine-learning model running in the cloud. The kit works offline, works on old hardware, and works in places where any of those dependencies would fail. The intelligence is in the design, not in the silicon.", "why": "Mainstream assistive technology assumes a user with money, infrastructure, and access to expensive devices. A trusted contact (family member, caregiver) receives live location and an alert if the system detects a fall or physiological distress. The user controls who sees what.

We've tested the kit in real-world conditions across multiple countries — different terrains, different climates, different sound environments. The same device behaves differently in every place. Third: open-sourcing the full build — schematics, firmware, training materials — so any community anywhere can manufacture locally.
